question: In 2022, Members of the European Parliament called for stricter rules on toys entering the EU from third countries and urged the Commission to adopt implementing measures laying down techniques for checks on the basis of common risk analysis at EU level.

The national authorities of the Member States will also be involved in the implementation of stricter controls on the movement of toys, and this issue was at the centre of discussions in the EU institutions in 2023, as shown by the adoption of the resolution on the implementation of the 2009 Directive. In light of this: 1.

Does the Commission intend to provide financial support to Member States in the setting up of bodies to improve checks on toys placed on the EU market, given that the creation of new monitoring bodies or the extension of the scope of existing ones would entail additional administrative and field work?
Does the Commission plan to create and implement a social media campaign to raise awareness among EU citizens about the dangers posed by chemical substances present in toys?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (29.5.2024) The Commission presented a proposal for a Regulation on the safety of toys on 28 July 20231 accompanied by an impact assessment2, following the Commission evaluation of the Toy Safety Directive3 as well as the subsequent European Parliament resolution on the Toy Safety Directive4.

To address the high number of non-compliant toys, the Commission proposed that all toys will have a digital product passport including information on the compliance of the toy, and that the existence of the product passport will be verified at customs when the toy is presented for release for free circulation.

This verification will happen automatically through an interconnection between the digital product passport registry and the national customs systems via the EU Customs Single Window Certificates Exchange System5. The Commission does not currently consider providing additional funding to market surveillance authorities.

The impact assessment accompanying the proposal6 calculated that the introduction of a digital product passport will lead to time savings for national authorities in inspections that would be in the range of 15% to 25% compared to the current situation under the Toy Safety Directive.

The average number of inspections in the EU is expected to rise by an additional 3 500 to 6 000 per year assuming the budget allocated by Member States for market surveillance in toys will remain the same and that the efficiency gains will be reinvested in additional toy inspections. The Commission shares the objective of raising awareness on toy safety in general, and risks coming from non-compliant toys.
A social media campaign on toys is not envisaged at the moment.
